Life imprisonment, advocates claim, achieves the same protective function as execution. This is demonstrably false.

Prisoners serving life sentences have killed correctional officers and fellow inmates. Some have escaped and killed again. Others have ordered murders from behind bars, directing criminal organizations or intimidating witnesses. Edmund Kemper, Dennis Rader, and numerous other killers continued to torment victims' families from prison through letters and media manipulation.

Moreover, sentences are not permanent. Parole boards change composition. Laws are reformed. Political climates shift. "Life without parole" has been converted to "life with parole" in various jurisdictions. In some countries, mass amnesties have released convicted murderers. Only execution provides absolute certainty that a killer will never harm another person.

The families of murder victims deserve to live without the perpetual anxiety that their loved one's killer might one day walk free through some unforeseen legal or political development. The death penalty provides a finality that no alternative can match.

The Deterrence Debate: Evidence Reconsidered

Critics frequently assert that capital punishment fails to deter crime, citing studies showing no clear correlation between execution rates and murder rates. However, this conclusion deserves serious scrutiny.

First, the methodological challenges in studying deterrence are immense. Murder rates are influenced by countless variables—economic conditions, drug epidemics, policing strategies, demographic shifts, and cultural factors. Isolating the effect of a rarely-applied punishment across different jurisdictions with varying implementation is extraordinarily difficult.

Second, several rigorous studies have found deterrent effects. Economists Hashem Dezhbakhsh, Paul Rubin, and Joanna Shepherd found that each execution, on average, prevented approximately eighteen murders. Studies by economists at Emory University, the University of Houston, and other institutions have reached similar conclusions. While the research remains contested, the confident assertion that "there is no deterrent effect" overstates the scholarly consensus.

Third, consider the logic: we believe that incentives and disincentives shape behavior in virtually every other domain. We fine speeding because we believe it reduces speeding. We imprison thieves because we believe it discourages theft. Why would rational actors contemplating the most serious crime—murder—be uniquely immune to considering the most serious consequence?

At minimum, the death penalty provides absolute specific deterrence: executed murderers have a zero percent recidivism rate. Given that approximately 1% of murderers who are released kill again, even modest use of capital punishment for the most dangerous offenders saves innocent lives mathematically.

Addressing the Wrongful Conviction Argument

The most powerful argument against capital punishment is the risk of executing the innocent. This concern is legitimate and demands serious response—but it is not dispositive.

The advent of DNA evidence, improved forensic techniques, enhanced due process protections, and multiple layers of appellate review have dramatically reduced the risk of wrongful conviction in capital cases. These cases receive more scrutiny, more resources, and more attention than any others in the criminal justice system. The standard of proof, while formally "beyond a reasonable doubt," is effectively higher in capital cases precisely because of the stakes involved.

Furthermore, the wrongful conviction argument proves too much. If the possibility of error means we cannot execute, why does it not mean we cannot imprison? A person wrongfully imprisoned for thirty years has suffered an immense injustice—years of life stolen, relationships destroyed, opportunities lost. If we accepted that any risk of error prohibits serious punishment, we would have to abandon the criminal justice system entirely.

The proper response to wrongful conviction risk is not abolition but reform: restricting capital punishment to cases with overwhelming evidence (multiple forms of physical evidence, clear video documentation, reliable confessions corroborated by independent facts), maintaining robust appeals processes, and funding innocence projects that use new evidence to review old convictions.

We should also consider the moral mathematics honestly. If abolishing the death penalty prevents one wrongful execution but—through eliminated deterrence and incapacitation—results in additional innocent people being murdered, have we actually honored the value of innocent life? This is not a comfortable calculation, but it is an honest one.

Opponents note that capital cases cost more than non-capital cases due to extended litigation. This is true under current systems—but it reflects policy choices, not inherent necessities.

Much of the additional cost stems from decades of procedural complexity added by courts skeptical of capital punishment. These procedures could be streamlined while maintaining essential due process protections. Additionally, comparing the cost of a capital case to a non-capital case is the wrong comparison; the relevant comparison is to the cost of lifetime incarceration, which in many jurisdictions exceeds $1 million per inmate when accounting for geriatric medical care and decades of housing, food, and security.

More fundamentally, justice should not be primarily a cost-benefit calculation. We do not ask whether it is "cost-effective" to investigate murders or prosecute rapists. We accept these as obligations of a just society. If capital punishment is morally warranted, its costs are the costs of justice.

Critics note that most Western democracies have abolished capital punishment and that international human rights bodies oppose it. This deserves several responses.

First, the practices of other nations are not automatically correct. Many of these same nations have adopted policies—on speech, self-defense, or religious accommodation—that Americans reasonably reject. Democratic sovereignty means the American people can make their own judgments about justice.

Second, global public opinion is less abolitionist than elite opinion. When polled, citizens in many abolitionist countries express support for capital punishment, suggesting that abolition often reflects judicial or political elite preferences rather than democratic consensus.

Third, international human rights instruments that prohibit capital punishment typically prohibit arbitrary deprivation of life, not deprivation of life following due process for the gravest crimes. The death penalty has coexisted with human rights principles throughout modern history.

Beyond philosophical arguments, capital punishment serves an expressive function that no alternative matches. When society executes a murderer, it makes an unambiguous statement: this crime was so terrible that the perpetrator has forfeited everything. This is not vengeance—it is recognition.

For victims' families, the death penalty can provide something that life imprisonment cannot: a definitive ending. While no punishment can restore what was lost, execution marks a completion, a closing of the account. Families need not spend decades contemplating their loved one's killer living, eating, breathing while their victim cannot.

Society, too, benefits from this moral clarity. The death penalty draws a bright line that affirms our deepest values. It declares that innocent human life is so precious that deliberately taking it carries the ultimate consequence. Abolishing capital punishment, by contrast, suggests that no crime—no matter how monstrous—truly merits the most serious response human law can provide.

Capital punishment is not a relic of barbarism but a reflection of civilization's highest commitment: that justice must be done, that the innocent must be protected, and that some acts place their perpetrators beyond the ordinary boundaries of human community.

A society that cannot bring itself to execute the terrorist who murders hundreds, the predator who tortures children, or the killer who takes life after life has not achieved moral enlightenment—it has achieved moral confusion. It has prioritized the life of the guilty over the lives of the innocent, the comfort of the murderer over the memory of the murdered.

Properly limited to the most heinous crimes, carefully applied with robust procedural protections, and honestly acknowledged as the grave and serious act it is, capital punishment remains what it has always been: a necessary tool of justice, a proportionate response to ultimate evil, and a society's final declaration that innocent life matters more than guilty life.

The death penalty should not only be retained but applied with renewed commitment—not from bloodlust, but from a sober recognition that justice sometimes demands nothing less.

Justice Served: The Moral and Practical Case for Capital Punishment

Introduction

The question of whether the state possesses the moral authority to impose the ultimate sanction—the death penalty—has been debated by philosophers, legal scholars, and citizens for centuries. While opponents of capital punishment argue from the positions of human rights, fallibility of the justice system, and the sanctity of life, a careful and reasoned examination of the evidence reveals that capital punishment remains not only justified but essential to a functioning system of justice. When reserved for the most heinous crimes and applied through rigorous evidentiary standards, capital punishment serves the causes of justice, deterrence, public safety, and moral order. To abandon it is to weaken the very foundation upon which civilized society rests: proportional justice.

I. The Moral Foundation: Proportional Justice

At the heart of every legal system lies a principle so fundamental that it predates written law—the principle of proportionality. Justice demands that the punishment fit the crime. A parking ticket for a serial murderer is not merciful; it is an abdication of moral responsibility. When a person deliberately and with malice aforethought takes the life of an innocent human being, the moral scale of justice requires the most severe reckoning available.

The concept of proportional retribution is not a modern invention. It is woven into the fabric of Western moral philosophy, from the lex talionis of the Code of Hammurabi to the ethical frameworks of Immanuel Kant, who argued that murderers must die because no alternative punishment satisfies the demands of justice. Kant wrote that if justice perishes, then it is no longer worth it that men should live on earth. This is not a cry for vengeance—it is a recognition that moral order requires a response commensurate with the severity of the offense.

Consider, for example, those who commit atrocities so grotesque that lesser punishments become morally absurd: the premeditated torture and murder of children, the mass execution of innocent civilians by terrorists, the serial killing of multiple victims over years of calculated cruelty. In such cases, life imprisonment does not adequately express society's moral condemnation. It reduces the value of the victims' lives by suggesting that the ultimate crime can be answered with anything short than the ultimate penalty. Capital punishment, properly applied, affirms that some acts are so morally reprehensible that the perpetrator forfeits the right to continue living among us—not out of hatred, but out of a profound respect for the value of the lives that were destroyed.

Furthermore, the concept of human dignity cuts both ways. Opponents of capital punishment often argue that the death penalty violates the dignity of the condemned. But what of the dignity of the victims? What of the dignity of a society that tells a grieving parent that the person who tortured and killed their child is being housed, fed, and entertained at public expense for the rest of their natural life? True compassion must extend to those who suffer the worst losses imaginable, and justice for victims demands a response that acknowledges the absolute enormity of what was done to them.

II. The Deterrence Argument: Saving Innocent Lives

Beyond moral philosophy lies the empirical question: does capital punishment deter crime? While the debate continues in academic circles, a growing body of evidence suggests that it does, and the logic underlying its deterrent effect is compelling.

Economists and criminologists, including those who have published in peer-reviewed journals such as the Journal of Law and Economics, have found statistically significant correlations between the implementation of the death penalty and reductions in homicide rates. A landmark 2003 study by Hashem Dezhbakhsh, Paul Rubin, and Joanna Shepherd at Emory University concluded that each execution results in, on average, eighteen fewer murders, with a margin of error of ten to twenty-four. Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of Colorado, the University of Houston, and other institutions have produced similar findings.

Critics of deterrence studies often point to the difficulty of isolating the death penalty's effect from other variables—poverty levels, policing strategies, incarceration rates, and cultural attitudes toward violence. This is a legitimate methodological concern, but it does not negate the cumulative weight of evidence. Moreover, the argument that deterrence cannot be conclusively proven works against the abolitionist position as well. If we cannot prove that the death penalty deters, neither can we prove that it does not. In a reasonable assessment of risk, the possibility that the death penalty saves innocent lives should weigh heavily in the calculus. If even one execution prevents one murder—one innocent person alive who otherwise would be dead—the moral case for retaining the penalty becomes extraordinarily strong, because the lives of potential victims carry at least as much moral weight as the lives of convicted murderers.

The logic of deterrence is intuitive. Human beings are, by nature, responsive to incentives and disincentives. We know this from every other area of law and regulation. Traffic fines reduce speeding. Tax penalties reduce fraud. The more severe the potential consequence, the more powerful the deterrent signal—at least for rational actors who weigh costs and benefits before committing crimes of planning and premeditation. Many capital murders—contract killings, murders for insurance, gang-related executions—are committed by individuals who deliberately weigh risks. For such individuals, the prospect of execution is meaningfully different from and more consequential than the prospect of life in prison.

Even if we grant the most conservative reading of the data—that deterrence is marginal and uncertain—the argument for capital punishment does not depend on deterrence alone. It is supported simultaneously by retributive justice, incapacitation, and the moral order of society. The deterrence evidence simply adds a consequentialist dimension to an already robust moral case.

III. The Irreplaceable Safeguard of Public Safety

Another overwhelmingly practical argument for capital punishment is permanent incapacitation. A person sentenced to death can never harm another person—not a fellow inmate, not a prison guard, not a visitor, and not a member of the general public.

The history of even maximum-security incarceration is punctuated by cases of convicted murderers who killed again. Prison murders, both of inmates and correctional officers, are a persistent reality. In 2015, two convicted murderers who had been serving life sentences escaped from the Clinton Correctional Facility in New York, prompting a massive manhunt. Richard Matt, already convicted of murder, and David Sweat, who had killed a sheriff's deputy, demonstrated that even the most tightly controlled prison environments cannot guarantee that violent offenders will never again pose a threat.

Some might argue that life imprisonment without the possibility of parole (LWOP) provides the same level of public safety. In theory, perhaps. But in practice, legal landscapes change. Parole boards occasionally grant release to convicted murderers. Sentences are reduced on appeal. Legislation is enacted that reclassifies what constitutes "life" behind bars. Governors issue commutations. The legal system is, by design, dynamic—and that dynamism introduces risk. Capital punishment is the only sentence that absolutely and irrevocably ensures that a convicted murderer will never kill again.

This is not a hypothetical concern. There are numerous documented cases of individuals who murdered multiple victims, were convicted and sentenced only to later kill again—either in prison or after release. The permanence of the death penalty eliminates this risk entirely and provides an ironclad guarantee that society's worst predators will never again threaten the innocent.

IV. Addressing the Argument of Irreversible Error

No honest defense of capital punishment can dismiss the gravity of wrongful conviction. The possibility that an innocent person might be executed is deeply troubling, and it deserves serious engagement rather than casual dismissal.

However, this argument, while emotionally potent, does not withstand rigorous scrutiny as a reason to abolish capital punishment entirely.

First, the American legal system already employs the most extensive safeguards of any justice system in human history to prevent wrongful executions. Capital cases involve bifurcated trials, mandatory appeals, habeas corpus review, and increasingly sophisticated forensic standards. The advent of DNA technology has revolutionized the ability to establish guilt with near-certainty. Since the advent of post-conviction DNA testing, it has become possible to exclude suspects and confirm guilt at a level of reliability unimaginable a generation ago. As forensic technology continues to advance—touch DNA, genealogical databases, digital evidence analysis—the margin of error continues to shrink.

Second, the argument from fallibility proves too much. Every system of punishment is fallible. Innocent people are wrongly convicted of non-capital crimes and spend years—even decades—in prison, enduring suffering that can never be undone. The remedy for wrongful incarceration is not to eliminate imprisonment but to strengthen the safeguards that prevent it. Similarly, the remedy for the risk of wrongful execution is not to eliminate the death penalty but to ensure that it is applied only in cases of overwhelming evidence and through the most rigorous legal processes available.

Third, the actual scale of wrongful executions in the United States has been wildly exaggerated by advocacy organizations. While the Innocence Project has documented instances of wrongful conviction, claims that dozens or scores of innocent people have been executed are not supported by credible evidence. Samuel Gross of the University States, in a widely cited but frequently misrepresented study, estimated a wrongful conviction rate among death row defendants of approximately 4.1 percent—but his category of wrongful conviction includes defendants who had their convictions overturned or who were exonerated, not defendants who were actually executed in error. The rigorous, case-by-case examination of historical executions conducted by legal scholars has found precious few cases where the executed individual was plausibly innocent.

Ultimately, the risk of error, while it must be minimized at every turn, does not morally compel the abolition of any penalty. It compels us to be vigilant, thorough, and just. Abolition would mean sacrificing justice for the guilty on the altar of avoiding a risk that, while real, has been amplified beyond its actual proportions.

V. Justice for Victims and Their Families

Every serious discussion of capital punishment must center the experience of victims and their families. For those who have lost loved ones to premeditated, brutal murder, the justice system offers one of the few mechanisms through which their profound suffering can be formally acknowledged and addressed.

A death sentence communicates something that no other verdict can: that society recognizes the absolute wrongness of what was done, that the victim's life mattered, and that the magnitude of the crime warrants the most serious sanction civilization possesses. For many families of murder victims, the death penalty offers not revenge but a measure of closure—the knowledge that the person responsible has been held fully accountable and will never again bring suffering to another family.

The suffering of victims' families is not merely emotional; it is economic, psychological, and social. A landmark study published in the Marquette Law Review found that families of murder victims in states without the death penalty reported significantly lower levels of satisfaction with the criminal justice system and greater psychological distress compared to families in states where the death penalty is available and applied. While the death penalty does not heal all wounds—it cannot bring back the dead—it validates the victim's life and the survivor's loss in a way that other sentences cannot.

When the state imposes a life sentence without parole in place of the ultimate penalty, many families experience a secondary form of trauma—the sense that their loved one has been devalued, that the killer's life is deemed comparable in worth to the victim's death. Capital punishment, by contrast, honors the dead and serves those who grieve them.

VI. The Role of Capital Punishment in Moral Order

The death penalty also serves a broader symbolic and pedagogical function within society. Legal systems are not merely mechanisms for settling disputes and punishing wrongdoers; they are expressions of collective moral values. When a society declares that certain acts are so unconscionable that they warrant the forfeiture of the perpetrator's life, it communicates a standard of moral seriousness that shapes the behavior and attitudes of its citizens.

In a world where evil exists—where individuals deliberately and maliciously destroy innocent human life for pleasure, profit, or ideology—the law must be capable of expressing the profound moral gravity of those acts. The death penalty stands as a definitive statement that there are limits to human conduct beyond which a person cannot pass without forfeiting his or her claim to continued life within the community of civilized beings.

This is not about vengeance. It is about maintaining the moral clarity that sustains a just society. As the great legal scholar and jurist Robert Blecker has argued in his extensive comparative study The Death Penalty as Punishment, the most severe punishments are owed to the worst offenders. To punish the worst crimes with anything less than the severest available penalty corrupts the moral message of the law and risks normalizing the evil acts it condemns.

VII. Comparative and Historical Perspective

The use of capital punishment is neither an aberration nor a relic of a barbaric past. It has been employed across cultures and civilizations for millennia—not out of cruelty, but out of the recognition that justice requires proportionality. In the modern era, the majority of the world's democracies—including the United States, Japan, India, and many Caribbean nations—retain the death penalty in law, even if its application varies.

International movements toward abolition, while significant, do not represent a universal moral consensus. The European Union's abolitionist stance is a regional preference, not an internationally binding norm. The United Nations General Assembly resolutions calling for a moratorium on the death penalty are non-binding and have been voted against or abstained on by a significant number of member states. The global picture is more nuanced than abolitionist advocates suggest, and the persistence of capital punishment in some of the world's largest and most stable democracies reflects a considered judgment that this penalty remains a legitimate component of a just legal order.

Moreover, public opinion within the United States—while more divided than it was fifty years ago—continues to show substantial majority support for capital punishment, particularly when respondents are presented with specific, aggravated murder scenarios. This is not mob mentality; it is the considered moral intuition of millions of citizens who recognize that justice sometimes demands the ultimate sanction.

VIII. Prudent Expansion: Where the Conversation Must Go

A persuasive case for capital punishment today is not merely a defense of the status quo—it is an argument for thoughtful expansion. The evidence regarding deterrence, incapacitation, and retributive justice suggests that the death penalty is currently underutilized relative to the threat that the most dangerous criminals pose to society.

Current application of capital punishment is uneven and often inconsistent. In some jurisdictions, particularly those with progressive prosecutors and governors who have imposed moratoriums, the death penalty has become de facto unavailable, even for the most egregious offenders. This inconsistency undermines the deterrent effect of the penalty and creates geographical lottery in justice—where the fate of a convicted murderer depends not on the gravity of their crime but on the political climate of the state in which they were tried.

A more thoughtful approach would involve:

  • Expanding eligible categories to include large-scale drug trafficking that results in mass deaths, terrorism that deliberately targets civilians, and repeat violent offenders who demonstrate a pattern of lethal escalation.

  • Streamlining the appeals process to reduce the unconscionable decades-long delays that currently separate sentence from execution. These delays, which often stretch beyond twenty years, serve no legitimate purpose—they do not make the process more accurate, they do not enhance justice, and they compound the suffering of victims' families. While thorough review must be guaranteed, there is no moral justification for allowing legal inertia to stretch justice into a cruel and indefinite limbo.

  • Investing in forensic infrastructure to ensure that every capital case benefits from the most advanced investigative and scientific techniques available, reducing the already small risk of wrongful conviction to near zero.

  • Reinstating capital punishment in states that currently do not practice it but where the penalty remains popular and where organized crime, cartel violence, and mass-casualty offenses continue to produce extraordinarily dangerous offenders.

Such expansion must be accompanied by continued vigilance, rigorous oversight, and a commitment to applying the penalty only in cases where guilt is established beyond any reasonable doubt. The goal is not gratuitous severity but just proportionality.

Conclusion

Capital punishment is not a relic of a primitive past—it is a necessary, moral, and effective instrument of justice whose continued and expanded application serves the highest values of a civilized society. It expresses the proportional gravity of the most heinous crimes. It deters potential offenders from committing the worst acts humans can inflict upon one another. It permanently protects society from its most dangerous members. It offers the families of victims a measure of justice and closure. And it reinforces the moral order that distinguishes a just society from a lawless one.

None of this requires us to be blind to the imperfections of the system or to dismiss the gravity of death as a punishment. The very severity of capital punishment demands that it be applied with the utmost care, the highest evidentiary standards, and the most rigorous legal safeguards. But the imperative to be cautious does not translate into a mandate to surrender.

Abolitionists ask us to trust that a system without the death penalty can deliver justice. For ordinary crimes, it can. The Ultimate Sanction: A Case for the Moral and Practical Necessity of Capital Punishment

The debate surrounding capital punishment is one of the most enduring and emotionally charged discussions in modern jurisprudence and ethics. While abolitionist arguments often rely on concerns regarding irreversible error, the potential for bias, and questions of humane treatment, these concerns, while valid, must be weighed against the fundamental obligations of a just society: to protect its citizens, to uphold the moral order, and to ensure that justice is proportionate to the crime. The Moral Imperative of Retributive Justice

At the heart of the argument for capital punishment lies the principle of lex talionis, or the law of retaliation. This is not merely a call for vengeance, but a foundational concept of justice which dictates that the punishment must fit the crime. In cases of heinous, premeditated murder—particularly those involving torture, the killing of children, or acts of terrorism—the moral scales are tipped so violently that no lesser penalty can restore equilibrium.

Life imprisonment, while severe, fails to capture the gravity of taking an innocent life. It allows the perpetrator to continue existing, to eat, to sleep, and potentially to find comfort or purpose within the prison system, despite having extinguished the future of their victim. Capital punishment serves as the only proportional response to the ultimate violation of human rights: the intentional destruction of another human being. By imposing the death penalty, society affirms the intrinsic value of the victim’s life. Deterrence and the Protection of Society

Critics often argue that capital punishment does not deter crime, citing studies with conflicting results. However, this perspective overlooks the nuanced reality of human behavior and the specific contexts in which the death penalty is applied. While it may not deter crimes of passion or those committed under the influence of substances, it serves as a powerful deterrent against premeditated, calculated violence. Professional hitmen, terrorist planners, and serial killers operate with a degree of rationality; the prospect of losing their own lives introduces a ultimate consequence that life imprisonment does not.

Furthermore, the expansion of capital punishment can serve a critical incapacitation function. Every executed offender is an offender who will never kill again. Life imprisonment carries the inherent risk of escape, parole error, or violence within the prison system against guards and other inmates. By ensuring that the most dangerous individuals are permanently removed from society, capital punishment provides an absolute guarantee of public safety that no other sentence can offer. In an era where prison overcrowding and resource allocation are significant challenges, directing resources toward the rehabilitation of non-violent offenders rather than the lifelong containment of irredeemable monsters is a more efficient and morally sound allocation of societal resources.

Justice for Victims and Their Families

The criminal justice system exists not only to punish the guilty but to provide closure and justice for the victims and their families. For many survivors of violent crime, the knowledge that the perpetrator remains alive, regardless of the conditions of their confinement, is a source of ongoing trauma. The finality of capital punishment offers a definitive end to the legal process, allowing families to begin the healing process without the fear of parole hearings, appeals, or the possibility of release.

This is not about satisfying a bloodlust, but about acknowledging the profound and permanent loss suffered by the victims’ loved ones. When the state fails to impose the ultimate penalty for the ultimate crime, it sends a message to these families that their suffering is not fully recognized. Expanding the use of capital punishment in clear-cut cases of egregious murder restores faith in the system’s ability to deliver true justice, reinforcing the social contract between the state and its citizens.

Addressing Concerns: Rigor, Not Abolition

Opponents of capital punishment frequently cite the risk of executing the innocent. This is a serious concern, but it is an argument for reform, not abolition. With advancements in forensic science, particularly DNA testing, the accuracy of convictions has improved dramatically. The solution is not to discard a vital tool of justice but to implement stricter procedural safeguards, higher standards of evidence, and more rigorous appellate processes. By expanding the use of capital punishment within a framework of enhanced scientific and legal scrutiny, society can minimize error while maximizing justice.

Moreover, the argument that capital punishment is applied unfairly due to racial or socioeconomic biases is a critique of the administration of justice, not the principle itself. These disparities highlight the need for systemic reform in legal representation and prosecutorial discretion, not the elimination of the penalty. To abandon capital punishment because of implementation flaws is akin to abolishing surgery because of medical malpractice; the goal should be to improve the system, not to deny patients the cure.

Conclusion

Capital punishment is not a relic of a barbarous past, but a necessary component of a mature and morally coherent justice system. It affirms the sanctity of innocent life, provides a proportional response to the most heinous crimes, deters premeditated violence, and offers closure to victims’ families. While the application of the death penalty must be approached with caution, rigor, and fairness, its abolition would represent a retreat from justice rather than an advancement of human rights.

Society has a duty to protect its citizens and uphold the moral order. By continuing and expanding the use of capital punishment for the most egregious crimes, we affirm that some actions are so morally bankrupt that they forfeit the right to exist within the community. In doing so, we do not descend into barbarism; we rise to the occasion of true justice.
